title: Sampling Switches
intro: The simplest sampler is a MOS switch and a capacitor: the output tracks the input while the clock is high and freezes when it falls. The switch's on-resistance depends on the signal, which sets the usable swing and the speed (Razavi, Sections 13.2.1 and 13.2.2).

blocks.alt: A sampling switch controlled by a clock connects the input Vin to the output node Vout. A hold capacitor CH connects from the output node to ground.
blocks.caption: A switch and a capacitor make the simplest sample-and-hold circuit.

blocks.text: The MOS transistor as a switch

A MOSFET can be on while carrying no current, which is exactly what a sampler needs. It conducts in both directions, the terminal at the lower potential (for NMOS) acting as source. If $C_H$ starts at $V_{DD}$ and the input is at 0, the device first saturates and then discharges $C_H$ in the triode region all the way to 0; if the input is above the stored value it charges $C_H$ up to the input. Once settled, input and output are equal: the switch has no DC offset, unlike a bipolar sampler. Near the end of settling it behaves as a resistor:
The input range of a single switch

If the input approaches $V_{DD}$, the overdrive vanishes as the output rises: with $V_{in} = V_{DD}$ the device stays saturated and the output creeps toward $V_{DD} - V_{TH}$ ever more slowly (only subthreshold current finishes the job). In general $R_{on}$ blows up as $V_{in} \to V_{DD} - V_{TH}$, and the threshold, raised further by body effect, eats directly into the swing. A PMOS switch fails in the mirror-image way, as the input falls toward $|V_{THP}|$.

Speed must be quoted with an accuracy: the time for the output to come within a band $\Delta V$ of a full-scale step. With one time constant $\tau = R_{on}C_H$, settling to a fraction $\epsilon$ takes $\tau\ln(1/\epsilon)$; for half an LSB of an $N$-bit system, $t = (N+1)\ln 2\,\tau$. A large $W/L$ and a small $C_H$ are fast, but $R_{on}$ is largest for the highest input, so that sets the time constant. Allowing $R_{on}$ to vary by at most 4:1 limits the input to
which is close to $V_{DD}/2$: a severe limit set by the threshold, not by an overdrive.

blocks.text: An NMOS in parallel with a PMOS, driven by complementary clocks, covers rail-to-rail inputs. Where both conduct,

blocks.tex: R_{on,eq} = \frac{1}{\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_N (V_{DD} - V_{THN}) - \left[\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_N - \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_P\right]V_{in} - \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_P |V_{THP}|}

blocks.text: If $\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_N = \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_P$ the $V_{in}$ term cancels and $R_{on,eq}$ is flat (body effect spoils this somewhat). The two devices must turn off at the same instant: if the NMOS opens $\Delta t$ early, the PMOS keeps tracking for $\Delta t$ with a large, signal-dependent time constant, which distorts the sample. A simple fix for moderate accuracy derives the two clocks so that the delay of the inverter making $\overline{CK}$ is matched by a pass gate in the $CK$ path. (Bootstrapped switches, which hold $V_{GS}$ constant by riding the gate on the input, are the common high-linearity alternative.)

blocks.title: On-resistance over the swing
blocks.text: An NMOS switch has $\mu_n C_{ox} = 200\,\mu$A/V², $W/L = 20$, $V_{TH} = 0.45$ V and its gate at $V_{DD} = 1.8$ V. Find $R_{on}$ at $V_{in} = 0$, 0.3 V and 0.6 V, and the largest input that keeps $R_{on}$ within 4:1 of its minimum.

blocks.title: Settling time
blocks.text: A sampling switch has $R_{on} = 1$ kΩ driving $C = 1$ pF. How long to settle to within half an LSB of a 10-bit converter?
solution: Error below half an LSB of 10 bits means $e^{-t/\tau} < 2^{-11}$, so $t = 11\ln 2\,\tau = 7.6$ ns.

blocks.title: A flat transmission gate
blocks.text: A complementary switch has $\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_N = \mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_P = 2$ mA/V², $V_{DD} = 1.8$ V and both thresholds 0.5 V. Find $R_{on,eq}$ for inputs where both devices are on, and the range over which that holds.
solution: With equal factors, $R_{on,eq} = 1/[k(V_{DD} - V_{THN} - |V_{THP}|)] = 1/(2\text{ mA/V}^2 \times 0.8\text{ V}) = 625$ Ω.
Both are on for $|V_{THP}| < V_{in} < V_{DD} - V_{THN}$, i.e. 0.5 V to 1.3 V; outside it one device alone conducts with lower resistance.
